title: Worst case response time analysis of sporadic graph tasks with fixed priority scheduling on a uniprocessor

extraction.paper_name: Worst case response time analysis of sporadic graph tasks with fixed priority scheduling on a uniprocessor
extraction.paper_description: This paper extends worst-case response time (WCRT) analysis for sporadic graph tasks under fixed-priority scheduling on a uniprocessor. It covers preemptive, non-preemptive, and hybrid scheduling scenarios, transforming graph tasks into canonical chains and defining feasibility conditions based on WCRT computation for individual subtasks and the overall graph task.

formal_description.statement: A sporadic graph task tau_i is defined by: G_i, T_i, D_i. G_i_tau_i = {tau_i_1, ..., tau_i_ni} is the set of ni subtasks composing the graph G_i.

variables.G_i: A graph of subtasks with precedence constraints
variables.T_i: The minimum inter-arrival time (period) of the graph task
variables.D_i: The relative deadline of the graph task (a graph task released at time t must be executed by its absolute deadline t + D_i)
variables.G_i_tau_i: The set of subtasks belonging to graph G_i
variables.ni: The number of subtasks in graph G_i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the fundamental properties of a sporadic graph task.

informal_sketch.intuition: A sporadic graph task represents an application with multiple interconnected subtasks. It has a minimum time between its releases (period) and a deadline by which all its subtasks must complete.
steps: Identify the graph structure (G_i) representing subtasks and their dependencies.
Note the minimum time between consecutive releases of this graph task (T_i).
Note the deadline relative to its release time (D_i) by which the entire graph task must finish.
key_insights: Graph tasks model complex applications with internal parallelism and dependencies.
Sporadic nature means releases are not strictly periodic but have a minimum inter-arrival time.

formal_description.statement: A subtask tau_i_j of a graph task tau_i is defined by: C_i_j, T_i, pi_i_j. A partial order tau_i_j < tau_i_k means tau_i_j must be completed before tau_i_k.

variables.tau_i_j: The j-th subtask of graph task tau_i
variables.T_i: The minimum inter-arrival time (period), inherited from its graph task tau_i
variables.pi_i_j: The fixed priority of subtask tau_i_j (0 is the highest priority)
variables.tau_i_j < tau_i_k: Precedence constraint: tau_i_j must complete before tau_i_k can start

assumptions: Time is discrete (parameters are multiples of clock tick)
Subtasks can be preemptive or non-preemptive
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the properties of individual subtasks within a graph task.

informal_sketch.intuition: Each subtask is a basic unit of work with a specific execution time and a priority. It inherits the release characteristics of its parent graph task and must respect any dependencies with other subtasks in the graph.
steps: Assign an execution time (C_i_j) to each subtask.
Assign a fixed priority (pi_i_j) to each subtask, where lower numerical values mean higher priority.
Establish precedence relationships: if subtask A must finish before subtask B starts, record A < B.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
class Subtask:
    def __init__(self, parent_task_id, subtask_id, execution_time, priority):
        self.parent_task_id = parent_task_id
        self.subtask_id = subtask_id
        self.C = execution_time
        self.T = None # Inherited from parent task
        self.pi = priority
        self.predecessors = []
        self.successors = []
key_insights: Subtasks are the atomic units of scheduling within a graph task.
Priorities determine scheduling order among ready subtasks.
Precedence constraints enforce logical execution order.

results.identifier: Definition 3: Idle Period and Busy Period

formal_description.statement: An idle time t is defined on a processor as a time, such that there are no subtasks released before time t pending at time t. An interval of successive idle times is called an idle period. A busy period is defined as a time interval [a,b), such that there is no idle time in [a,b) (the processor is fully busy) and such that both a and b are idle times.

variables.a: Start time of a busy period
variables.b: End time of a busy period

formal_description.conclusion: Defines fundamental concepts for analyzing processor utilization and task execution intervals.

informal_sketch.intuition: An idle period is when the processor has nothing to do. A busy period is when the processor is continuously working, from the moment a task becomes ready until all pending tasks are completed and the processor becomes idle again.
steps: Identify points in time where no subtasks are waiting or executing (idle times).
A sequence of such idle times forms an idle period.
An interval where the processor is continuously executing tasks, bounded by idle times, is a busy period.
key_insights: Busy periods are critical for response time analysis because they represent intervals of continuous contention for the processor.
The length of a busy period determines the maximum number of task activations that can occur within it.

formal_description.statement: P_i: the corresponding chain of graph G_i. P_i_j_star: the canonical chain. tau_i_j: the j-th task in the chain P_i. The canonical chain P_i_j_star is obtained by modifying priorities of tau_i_m (from m=j down to m=2) to pi_i_m if pi_i_m_minus_1 > pi_i_m, and combining consecutive subtasks with equal priority into a single subtask with summed execution duration.

variables.P_i: The linear chain of subtasks obtained from graph G_i by a specific transformation rule (highest priority subtask without predecessors is selected first).
variables.P_i_j_star: The canonical chain derived from P_i, specifically for analyzing subtask tau_i_j.
variables.tau_i_j: The j-th subtask in the chain P_i (after initial graph-to-chain transformation).

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the transformed representations of a graph task used for WCRT analysis.

informal_sketch.intuition: Graph tasks are complex, so they are simplified into a linear sequence (chain) of subtasks. For WCRT analysis of a specific subtask, this chain is further 'canonicalized' by adjusting priorities and merging subtasks to simplify interference calculations.
steps: **Graph to Chain (P_i):** Start with an empty chain. Repeatedly find subtasks with no predecessors, select the highest priority among them, add it to the chain, and remove it from the graph until the graph is empty.

**Chain to Canonical Chain (P_i_j_star) w.r.t. tau_i_j:** Iterate from subtask tau_i_j backwards to tau_i_2. If the priority of the preceding subtask (tau_i_m_minus_1) is higher than the current subtask (tau_i_m), change tau_i_m_minus_1's priority to tau_i_m's priority. This ensures priorities are non-decreasing up to tau_i_j.
Merge consecutive subtasks in the canonical chain that have the same priority into a single subtask, summing their execution durations.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def transform_graph_to_chain(graph_G):
    chain_P = []
    remaining_subtasks = list(graph_G.subtasks)
    while remaining_subtasks:
        ready_subtasks = [s for s in remaining_subtasks if not s.predecessors_in_remaining(remaining_subtasks)]
        if not ready_subtasks: break # Should not happen for valid DAG
        highest_priority_subtask = min(ready_subtasks, key=lambda s: s.pi)
        chain_P.append(highest_priority_subtask)
        remaining_subtasks.remove(highest_priority_subtask)
    return chain_P

def transform_chain_to_canonical(chain_P, target_subtask_tau_i_j):
    canonical_chain = list(chain_P)
    j_index = canonical_chain.index(target_subtask_tau_i_j)
    for m_idx in range(j_index, 0, -1):
        tau_i_m = canonical_chain[m_idx]
        tau_i_m_minus_1 = canonical_chain[m_idx - 1]
        if tau_i_m_minus_1.pi > tau_i_m.pi:
            tau_i_m_minus_1.pi = tau_i_m.pi # Adjust priority
    
    # Merge consecutive subtasks with equal priority
    merged_chain = []
    if not canonical_chain: return merged_chain
    current_merged_subtask = canonical_chain[0].copy()
    for i in range(1, len(canonical_chain)):
        if canonical_chain[i].pi == current_merged_subtask.pi:
            current_merged_subtask.C += canonical_chain[i].C
        else:
            merged_chain.append(current_merged_subtask)
            current_merged_subtask = canonical_chain[i].copy()
    merged_chain.append(current_merged_subtask)
    return merged_chain
key_insights: Simplifies complex graph structures into linear sequences for easier analysis.
The canonical chain ensures that the priorities of subtasks leading up to the studied subtask are non-decreasing, which simplifies interference calculations by allowing aggregation of work.

formal_description.statement: C_i_j_max: the longest execution duration of a subtask among those subtasks with lower priority than tau_i_j.

variables.C_i_j_max: The maximum execution time of any subtask in the system with a priority lower than pi_i_j_star (the priority of the currently studied subtask tau_i_j in its canonical chain).
variables.pi_i_j_star: The fixed priority of subtask tau_i_j in its canonical chain (from Definition 6).

formal_description.conclusion: Defines a system-wide blocking term used in non-preemptive and hybrid scheduling analysis.

informal_sketch.intuition: In non-preemptive scheduling, a lower priority subtask can block a higher priority one if it starts executing just before the higher priority subtask becomes ready. C_i_j_max captures the worst-case duration of such a blocking event from any lower priority subtask in the entire system.
steps: Identify the priority (pi_i_j_star) of the subtask tau_i_j being analyzed.
Scan all subtasks in the entire system (across all graph tasks).
Find all subtasks whose priority is numerically greater than pi_i_j_star (i.e., lower priority).
C_i_j_max is the maximum execution duration among these lower priority subtasks.
key_insights: This term is crucial for non-preemptive scheduling, as it quantifies the maximum blocking a high-priority subtask can experience from a lower-priority one.
It considers all subtasks in the system, not just those within the same graph task.

formal_description.statement: pi_i_j_paren: the lowest priority from the first subtask (tau_i_1) in the canonical chain to the subtask studied (tau_i_j). pi_i_j_star: the fixed priority of subtask tau_i_j in its canonical chain.

variables.pi_i_j_paren: The lowest (highest numerical value) priority among subtasks tau_i_1 to tau_i_j in the canonical chain P_i_j_star.
variables.pi_i_j_star: The priority of subtask tau_i_j after the canonical chain transformation.

formal_description.conclusion: Defines specific priority values used for segment grouping and busy period analysis in the canonical chain.

informal_sketch.intuition: These priorities are specific to the canonical chain. pi_i_j_star is simply the priority of the subtask being analyzed after canonicalization. pi_i_j_paren represents the 'effective' priority level of the entire prefix of the canonical chain up to tau_i_j, which is important for defining busy periods.
steps: **For pi_i_j_star:** After transforming P_i into P_i_j_star, the priority of tau_i_j in this new chain is pi_i_j_star.

**For pi_i_j_paren:** Examine all subtasks from tau_i_1 to tau_i_j in the canonical chain P_i_j_star. Find the subtask with the numerically largest priority value (lowest priority). This value is pi_i_j_paren.
key_insights: pi_i_j_star is the reference priority for segment classification.
pi_i_j_paren defines the priority level for which a busy period is considered, encompassing all subtasks up to tau_i_j in the canonical chain.

results.identifier: Definition 7: Segments (H, L, H_sb, H_mp, H_mb)

formal_description.statement: H_segment: A sub chain (segment) that comprises a sequence of consecutive subtasks having a priority greater than or equal to pi_i_j_star. L_segment: A sub chain (segment) that comprises a sequence of consecutive subtasks having a priority less than pi_i_j_star. H_sb: an H_segment which is preceded by an L_segment. H_mp: an H_segment which has no L_segment as predecessor. H_mb: an H_segment which follows immediately the subtask studied (tau_i_j).

variables.H_segment: A sequence of consecutive subtasks with priority >= pi_i_j_star
variables.L_segment: A sequence of consecutive subtasks with priority < pi_i_j_star
variables.H_sb: An H_segment that is preceded by an L_segment
variables.H_mp: An H_segment that is not preceded by an L_segment
variables.H_mb: An H_segment that immediately follows tau_i_j in the canonical chain
variables.pi_i_j_star: The fixed priority of subtask tau_i_j in its canonical chain (from Definition 6)

formal_description.conclusion: Classifies subtask sequences in the canonical chain and other chains based on their priority relative to the studied subtask, for interference analysis.

informal_sketch.intuition: To calculate interference, subtasks are grouped into segments based on their priority relative to the subtask being analyzed. 'H' segments have higher or equal priority and can interfere. 'L' segments have lower priority and generally don't interfere directly, but can cause blocking. The 'H' segments are further categorized by their position and preceding segments to distinguish different types of interference (preemption vs. blocking).
steps: For a given canonical chain (P_i_j_star) and other chains, and a studied subtask tau_i_j (with priority pi_i_j_star):
Identify H_segments: sequences of consecutive subtasks with priority >= pi_i_j_star.
Identify L_segments: sequences of consecutive subtasks with priority < pi_i_j_star.
Classify H_segments:
H_mp: If an H_segment is not immediately preceded by an L_segment (e.g., it's at the start of a chain or follows another H_segment). These cause preemption.
H_sb: If an H_segment is immediately preceded by an L_segment. These cause blocking (the L_segment must finish before the H_segment can run).
H_mb: If an H_segment immediately follows the studied subtask tau_i_j in its canonical chain. This causes multiple blocking if the chain is re-entrant.
key_insights: Segment classification simplifies the complex interactions between subtasks.
H_mp segments cause preemption, H_sb segments cause blocking, and H_mb segments cause 'multiple blocking' for re-entrant chains.

formal_description.statement: E_i_l_m: the total execution duration of a sub chain (segment) of subtasks from tau_i_l to tau_i_m. E_i_l_m = sum_{j=l}^{m} C_i_j

variables.E_i_l_m: Total execution duration of a segment of subtasks
variables.tau_i_l: The l-th subtask in the chain P_i
variables.tau_i_m: The m-th subtask in the chain P_i
variables.C_i_j: Execution duration of subtask tau_i_j (from Definition 2)

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the total execution time for a sequence of subtasks, typically a segment.

informal_sketch.intuition: When subtasks are grouped into segments, their individual execution times are summed up to get the total execution time of that segment. This simplifies calculations as the segment can be treated as a single unit of work.
steps: Identify the starting subtask (tau_i_l) and ending subtask (tau_i_m) of the segment.
Sum the execution durations (C_i_j) of all subtasks from tau_i_l to tau_i_m (inclusive).
key_insights: Allows treating segments as single computational units for workload calculations.
Essential for calculating interference from H_mp, H_sb, and H_mb segments.

formal_description.statement: E_i_1: the total execution duration of the first H_mp segment plus the H_mb segment of the chain studied.

variables.E_i_1: Total execution duration of specific segments within the canonical chain P_i_j_star.
variables.H_mp_first: The first H_mp segment in the canonical chain P_i_j_star.
variables.H_mb_segment: The H_mb segment in the canonical chain P_i_j_star (if it exists).

formal_description.conclusion: Defines a specific aggregated execution time used in workload calculations for the first subtask of a chain.

informal_sketch.intuition: This term aggregates the execution time of the initial high-priority segment and any 'multiple blocking' segment within the *same* canonical chain. It represents the work that must be done by the current chain itself, excluding the specific subtask being analyzed, but including parts that might be re-activated.
steps: Identify the first H_mp segment in the canonical chain P_i_j_star.
Calculate its total execution duration using Definition 8.
Identify the H_mb segment in P_i_j_star (if it exists).
Calculate its total execution duration using Definition 8.
Sum these two durations to get E_i_1.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_E_i_1(canonical_chain_P_i_j_star, target_subtask_tau_i_j):
    H_mp_segments, H_sb_segments, H_mb_segment = classify_segments(canonical_chain_P_i_j_star, get_pi_i_j_star(canonical_chain_P_i_j_star, target_subtask_tau_i_j), target_subtask_tau_i_j)
    
    first_H_mp_C = 0
    if H_mp_segments: # Assuming the first H_mp is the first segment of the chain if it's H_mp type
        first_H_mp_C = calculate_segment_execution_time(H_mp_segments[0])
    
    H_mb_C = 0
    if H_mb_segment:
        H_mb_C = calculate_segment_execution_time(H_mb_segment)
        
    return first_H_mp_C + H_mb_C
key_insights: Captures the self-interference and re-entrant blocking within the task's own canonical chain.
Used to account for the work of the current task that is not the specific instance of tau_i_j being studied, but still contributes to the busy period.

dependencies: Definition 7: Segments (H, L, H_sb, H_mp, H_mb)

formal_description.statement: MP: a set of segments of type H_mp and H_mb (if any). MP_j presents the MP set of subtask tau_i_j. SB: a set of segments of type H_sb.

variables.MP: Set of H_mp and H_mb segments from all chains (including the current one) that can interfere with tau_i_j.
variables.MP_j: The specific MP set relevant for subtask tau_i_j.
variables.SB: Set of H_sb segments from all chains (including the current one) that can interfere with tau_i_j.

formal_description.conclusion: Groups interfering segments into sets for easier calculation of preemption and blocking.

informal_sketch.intuition: These sets categorize all segments in the system that can interfere with the currently analyzed subtask. MP segments cause preemption (or re-entrant blocking), while SB segments cause blocking. This grouping simplifies the summation of interference terms.
steps: For a given subtask tau_i_j, identify all H_mp and H_mb segments from all graph tasks (including tau_i itself) that have priority >= pi_i_j_star. Collect them into the MP_j set.
Identify all H_sb segments from all graph tasks that have priority >= pi_i_j_star. Collect them into the SB set.
key_insights: MP segments contribute to preemption workload, as they can be activated multiple times.
SB segments contribute to blocking, as only one such segment can block the busy period start.

dependencies: Definition 7: Segments (H, L, H_sb, H_mp, H_mb)

formal_description.statement: A level tau_i_j busy period [a,b) is a time interval during which the processor is continuously processing at subtasks released in the interval [a,b) at priority level pi_i_j_paren or higher.

variables.a: Start time of the busy period
variables.b: End time of the busy period
variables.pi_i_j_paren: The lowest priority from tau_i_1 to tau_i_j in the canonical chain (from Definition 6)

formal_description.conclusion: Defines a busy period specific to a priority level, used for WCRT analysis.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is a specialized busy period. Instead of considering *all* tasks, it only considers tasks (or subtasks/segments) that have a priority equal to or higher than a specific threshold (pi_i_j_paren). This helps isolate the interference relevant to the subtask being analyzed.
steps: Identify the priority level pi_i_j_paren for the subtask tau_i_j.

A time interval [a,b) is a level tau_i_j busy period if, throughout this interval, the processor is continuously executing subtasks whose priority is >= pi_i_j_paren, and no such subtasks are pending at 'a' or 'b'.
key_insights: Focuses the busy period analysis on the specific priority level of interest, simplifying interference calculations.
This concept is fundamental to the iterative response time analysis technique.

results.identifier: Definition 12: Worst Case Level tau_i_j Busy Period

formal_description.statement: A worst case level tau_i_j busy period beginning at time t_0 is defined as a busy period where: P_i is active at time t_0. All the first subtasks of all the segments H_mp are released at time t_0. The longest blocking segment, chosen from all chains, happens at this time for the preemptive case. The longest blocking effect, chosen from the H_sb segment and those non preemptive subtasks, happens at this time for non preemptive and hybrid case.

variables.t_0: The start time of the worst-case busy period
variables.P_i: The chain of the graph task tau_i being studied

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the specific scenario that maximizes the length of a busy period, crucial for WCRT analysis.

informal_sketch.intuition: To find the worst-case response time, we need to find the longest possible busy period. This occurs when all interfering tasks and blocking events align perfectly at the start of the busy period, maximizing contention.
steps: Assume the busy period starts at t_0.
Assume the task P_i (containing tau_i_j) is released and active at t_0.
Assume all H_mp segments (from other tasks and P_i) are released at t_0, maximizing their preemption.
For preemptive case: Assume the single longest H_sb segment (from any task) blocks at t_0.
For non-preemptive/hybrid case: Assume the single longest blocking effect (from H_sb segments or any lower priority non-preemptive subtask) blocks at t_0.

formal_description.statement: L_i_j: the length of the worst case level tau_i_j busy period.

variables.L_i_j: The calculated length of the worst-case busy period for subtask tau_i_j.

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum duration the processor is busy with tasks of priority pi_i_j_paren or higher, under worst-case conditions.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is the key metric for determining how long a subtask might have to wait for higher priority work to complete. It's the solution to an iterative equation that sums up all the work that can occur at or above the subtask's priority level.
steps: Calculate L_i_j by solving an iterative equation (see Claim 3 or Claim 4) that sums the execution times of all higher priority interfering segments and blocking terms within a time interval of length L_i_j.
The smallest non-negative solution for L_i_j is the busy period length.
key_insights: L_i_j is a fundamental intermediate value for calculating response times.
It accounts for both direct execution and interference from other tasks/segments.

dependencies: Definition 12: Worst Case Level tau_i_j Busy Period

formal_description.statement: tau_i_j_k: the k-th activation of subtask tau_i_j in a given level tau_i_j busy period.

variables.tau_i_j_k: The k-th instance (job) of subtask tau_i_j.

formal_description.conclusion: Refers to a specific instance of a subtask within a busy period.

informal_sketch.intuition: During a long busy period, a sporadic task (and thus its subtasks) might be released multiple times. tau_i_j_k refers to the k-th such release and execution of subtask tau_i_j within that busy period.
steps: Identify the busy period.
Count the number of times subtask tau_i_j is released and becomes active within that busy period. The k-th count is tau_i_j_k.
key_insights: Response time analysis often needs to consider multiple instances of a task within a busy period, especially for tasks with deadlines greater than their periods.

formal_description.statement: W_i_j_k_t: the k-th instance workload of subtask tau_i_j. This is the amount of processing time of those subtasks with higher priority than tau_i_j whose release times are in the interval [0,t) for preemptive subtask and respectively [0,t] for non preemptive subtask.

variables.W_i_j_k_t: The total workload (execution time) that must be completed by time t for the k-th instance of tau_i_j to finish.
variables.t: A specific time point within the busy period.

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the cumulative processing demand up to time t for a specific instance of a subtask, including its own execution and interference.

informal_sketch.intuition: The workload at time 't' for a subtask instance is the sum of its own execution time, plus all the execution time of higher priority tasks that have been released and need to run before or by 't'. This is used to find the finish time: when the cumulative workload is less than or equal to the elapsed time 't'.
steps: For a given time 't' and the k-th instance of tau_i_j:
Sum the execution time of tau_i_j_k itself.
Sum the execution times of all higher priority subtasks (from all tasks) that are released within [0, t) (preemptive) or [0, t] (non-preemptive) and interfere with tau_i_j_k.
Include any blocking terms that occur at the start of the busy period.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_workload(t, target_tau_i_j_k, blocking_term, MP_set, E_i_1):
    workload = target_tau_i_j_k.subtask.C # Own execution
    workload += blocking_term # Initial blocking
    for segment_h in MP_set:
        # Interference from higher priority segments
        workload += ceil(t / segment_h.T) * segment_h.E
    # Additional terms for re-entrant chains (e.g., k * E_i_1)
    return workload
key_insights: Workload is the total processing demand that must be satisfied for a task instance to complete.
The interval for considering releases ([0,t) vs [0,t]) is a key difference between preemptive and non-preemptive analysis.

formal_description.statement: F_i_j_k: the finish time of the k-th instance of subtask tau_i_j.

variables.F_i_j_k: The absolute time at which the k-th instance of subtask tau_i_j completes its execution.

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the completion time of a specific subtask instance.

informal_sketch.intuition: The finish time is the earliest point in time when all the workload for a subtask instance (including its own execution and all higher priority interference) has been completed.
steps: For a given subtask instance tau_i_j_k, find the smallest time 't' such that the cumulative workload (W_i_j_k_t) is less than or equal to 't'. This 't' is F_i_j_k.
key_insights: Finish time is calculated iteratively, as interference depends on the length of the interval.
For subtasks with precedence, F_i_j_k depends on F_i_j_minus_1_k.

formal_description.statement: N_i: the activation number of chain P_i in this busy period. It is also the activation number of task studied in the chain P_i in this busy period. N_i = ceil(L_i_j / T_i)

variables.N_i: The maximum number of times the graph task tau_i (and thus its subtasks) can be activated within the worst-case busy period.
variables.L_i_j: The length of the worst-case level tau_i_j busy period (from Definition 13).
variables.T_i: The minimum inter-arrival time (period) of graph task tau_i (from Definition 1).

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum number of instances of a graph task that can contribute to the workload within a busy period.

informal_sketch.intuition: Once the length of the worst-case busy period (L_i_j) is known, we can determine how many times the graph task tau_i could be released within that period. This is simply the busy period length divided by the task's period, rounded up.
steps: Calculate the length of the worst-case busy period L_i_j (using Claim 3 or Claim 4).
Divide L_i_j by the period T_i of the graph task tau_i.
Round the result up to the nearest integer to get N_i.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_N_i(L_i_j, T_i):
    return ceil(L_i_j / T_i)
key_insights: N_i determines how many instances of tau_i_j (k=1 to N_i) need to have their finish times calculated to find the overall worst-case response time.
It directly links the busy period length to the number of task activations.

formal_description.statement: r_i_j: the worst case response time of any instance of subtask tau_i_j. r_i_j = max_{k=1...N_i} (F_i_j_k - (k-1)*T_i)

variables.r_i_j: The worst-case response time of subtask tau_i_j.
variables.N_i: The activation number of chain P_i (from Definition 17).
variables.F_i_j_k: The finish time of the k-th instance of subtask tau_i_j (from Definition 16).
variables.T_i: The minimum inter-arrival time (period) of graph task tau_i (from Definition 1).

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the maximum time from release to completion for any instance of a subtask.

informal_sketch.intuition: The response time of a task instance is its finish time minus its release time. Since tasks are released periodically (or sporadically with a minimum period), the k-th instance is released at (k-1)*T_i relative to the start of the busy period. We calculate this for all possible instances within the busy period and take the maximum to find the worst-case response time.
steps: For each instance k from 1 to N_i (the total number of activations in the busy period):
Calculate the finish time F_i_j_k (using Claim 6/7 or Claim 9/11).
Calculate the response time for this instance: F_i_j_k - (k-1)*T_i.
The worst-case response time r_i_j is the maximum of these individual instance response times.
key_insights: The worst-case response time is not necessarily the response time of the first instance.
It accounts for cumulative interference over multiple activations within a busy period.

formal_description.statement: The transformation of a graph G_i of a task tau_i into a chain P_i would not change the schedulability problem.
assumptions: The transformation rule (highest priority subtask without predecessors is selected first) is followed.
formal_description.conclusion: Analyzing the schedulability of the chain P_i is equivalent to analyzing the schedulability of the original graph G_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: The transformation process ensures that all precedence constraints are respected and that the relative priorities of subtasks are maintained. By always picking the highest priority ready subtask, the transformation effectively simulates the fixed-priority scheduling behavior, thus preserving schedulability properties.
steps: The transformation rule prioritizes subtasks based on their fixed priority and readiness (no predecessors).
This rule mimics how a fixed-priority scheduler would select tasks, ensuring that the critical path and interference patterns are preserved.
Therefore, if the chain is schedulable, the original graph is also schedulable, and vice-versa.
key_insights: Simplifies the analysis problem by converting a complex graph into a linear structure.
Relies on the specific graph-to-chain transformation rule to maintain equivalence.

formal_description.statement: The execution of a subtask tau_i_j and the execution duration of its canonical form tau_i_j_prime were the same.

variables.tau_i_j: Original subtask in the chain P_i (from Definition 4)
variables.tau_i_j_prime: The corresponding subtask in the canonical chain P_i_j_star (from Definition 4)

assumptions: The canonical chain transformation rule (priority adjustment and merging of equal-priority subtasks) is followed.
formal_description.conclusion: The total execution time of the subtask (or its merged equivalent in the canonical chain) remains unchanged.

informal_sketch.intuition: While priorities might be adjusted and subtasks merged in the canonical chain, the total amount of computation (execution duration) required for the original subtask, or the combined work it represents, remains constant. The transformation only changes how interference is viewed, not the fundamental work.
steps: The canonicalization process involves two main steps: priority adjustment and merging.
Priority adjustment does not change execution times.
Merging combines consecutive subtasks with equal priority by summing their execution durations. This means the *total* execution duration of the merged segment is preserved.
Therefore, the execution duration of tau_i_j (or the segment it becomes part of) is preserved.
key_insights: Ensures that the fundamental computational requirements are not altered by the canonicalization process.
Allows using the execution durations from the canonical chain for WCRT calculations.

formal_description.statement: L_i_j = sum_{h in MP} ceil(L_i_j / T_h) * E_h + max_{h in SB} E_h + C_i_1. This equation is solved by means of iterative computations for the smallest L_i_j.

variables.L_i_j: Length of the worst-case level tau_i_j busy period (from Definition 13).
variables.MP: Set of H_mp and H_mb segments (from Definition 10).
variables.T_h: Period of segment h (inherits from its graph task's period T_x).
variables.E_h: Total execution duration of segment h (from Definition 8).
variables.C_i_1: Execution duration of the first subtask tau_i_1 in the canonical chain P_i_j_star (from Definition 2).

assumptions: Preemptive scheduling.
Worst-case level tau_i_j busy period conditions (from Definition 12).
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an iterative equation to calculate the length of the worst-case busy period for a preemptive system.

informal_sketch.intuition: The busy period length is the sum of all work that needs to be done at or above the priority level of tau_i_j. This includes the execution of tau_i_1 (the first subtask of the current chain), blocking from one H_sb segment, and preemption from all H_mp/H_mb segments. Since preemption depends on the busy period length itself, it's an iterative calculation.
steps: Initialize L_i_j to an initial guess (e.g., C_i_1).
In each iteration, calculate the right-hand side (RHS) of the equation:
Sum the execution of all MP segments: For each segment 'h' in MP, calculate how many times it can be activated within L_i_j (ceil(L_i_j / T_h)) and multiply by its execution E_h.
Add the maximum blocking from SB segments: Find the largest E_h among all segments 'h' in SB.
Add the execution of the first subtask of the current chain, C_i_1.
Update L_i_j with the new RHS value.
Repeat until L_i_j converges (L_i_j_new == L_i_j_old). The smallest such L_i_j is the solution.
key_insights: The iterative nature handles the recursive dependency of interference on the busy period length.
The `ceil(L_i_j / T_h)` term accounts for multiple activations of higher priority tasks/segments.
Only one H_sb segment can block the start of the busy period in the preemptive case.

formal_description.statement: L_i_j = sum_{h in MP} ceil(L_i_j / T_h) * E_h + M_i_j + C_i_1. Where M_i_j = max(max_{h in SB} E_h, max_{m != i, pi_m < pi_i_j_star} C_m, C_i_j_max). This equation is solved by means of iterative computations for the smallest L_i_j.

variables.MP: Set of H_mp and H_mb segments (from Definition 10).
variables.T_h: Period of segment h (inherits from its graph task's period T_x).
variables.E_h: Total execution duration of segment h (from Definition 8).
variables.M_i_j: The maximum blocking term for non-preemptive/hybrid scheduling.
variables.C_m: Execution duration of subtask tau_m (from Definition 2).
variables.pi_i_j_star: Priority of subtask tau_i_j in its canonical chain (from Definition 6).
variables.C_i_j_max: Longest execution duration of a subtask with lower priority than tau_i_j (from Definition 5).
variables.C_i_1: Execution duration of the first subtask tau_i_1 in the canonical chain P_i_j_star (from Definition 2).

assumptions: Non-preemptive or hybrid scheduling.
Worst-case level tau_i_j busy period conditions (from Definition 12).
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an iterative equation to calculate the length of the worst-case busy period for non-preemptive or hybrid systems.

informal_sketch.intuition: Similar to the preemptive case, but the blocking term M_i_j is more comprehensive. It includes blocking from H_sb segments, blocking from any lower priority subtask from other chains, and a general system-wide maximum blocking from lower priority subtasks (C_i_j_max). This reflects the stronger blocking effect in non-preemptive environments.
steps: First, calculate the blocking term M_i_j:
Find the maximum E_h among all segments 'h' in SB.
Find the maximum C_m among all subtasks 'm' from *other* chains (m != i) whose priority pi_m is lower than pi_i_j_star.
Use C_i_j_max (the system-wide longest lower priority subtask execution).
M_i_j is the maximum of these three values.
Initialize L_i_j to an initial guess (e.g., C_i_1).
In each iteration, calculate the right-hand side (RHS) of the equation:
Sum the execution of all MP segments (same as Claim 3).
Add the calculated M_i_j blocking term.
Add the execution of the first subtask of the current chain, C_i_1.
Update L_i_j with the new RHS value.
Repeat until L_i_j converges. The smallest such L_i_j is the solution.
key_insights: The blocking term M_i_j is more complex due to non-preemptive effects, considering various sources of blocking.
The iterative solution method remains the same as in the preemptive case.

formal_description.statement: W_i_1_k_t = C_i_1 + M_i_1 + sum_{h in MP_1} ceil(t / T_h) * E_h + k * E_i_1. Where M_i_1 = max_{h in SB} E_h.

variables.W_i_1_k_t: Workload for the k-th instance of tau_i_1 at time t (from Definition 15).
variables.C_i_1: Execution duration of the first subtask tau_i_1 (from Definition 2).
variables.M_i_1: Blocking term for tau_i_1 in the preemptive case.
variables.MP_1: MP set for subtask tau_i_1 (from Definition 10).
variables.E_h: Execution duration of segment h (from Definition 8).
variables.E_i_1: Total execution duration of the first H_mp and H_mb segments of the current chain (from Definition 9).

assumptions: Preemptive scheduling.
Analyzing the first subtask tau_i_1 of the canonical chain.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the total processing demand for the k-th instance of the first subtask in a preemptive system.

informal_sketch.intuition: The workload for the first subtask includes its own execution, a blocking term from an H_sb segment, interference from all higher priority MP segments, and an additional term (k * E_i_1) to account for the re-entrant nature of the chain itself, where E_i_1 represents the work of the chain's initial segments that might be re-activated.
steps: Calculate M_i_1: the maximum execution duration among all H_sb segments.
Sum the execution of tau_i_1 (C_i_1).
Add M_i_1.
For each segment 'h' in MP_1, add its interference: ceil(t / T_h) * E_h.
Add the re-entrant chain effect: k * E_i_1.
key_insights: This formula captures all sources of demand and interference for the first subtask.
The `k * E_i_1` term is crucial for handling re-entrant graph tasks, where the initial part of the chain might be executed multiple times within a busy period.

results.identifier: Claim 6: Preemptive Finish Time for tau_i_1 (F_i_1_k)

formal_description.statement: F_i_1_k = min {t >= 0 | W_i_1_k_t <= t}

variables.F_i_1_k: Finish time of the k-th instance of tau_i_1 (from Definition 16).
variables.W_i_1_k_t: Workload for the k-th instance of tau_i_1 at time t (from Claim 5).

assumptions: Preemptive scheduling.
Analyzing the first subtask tau_i_1 of the canonical chain.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an iterative equation to calculate the finish time of the k-th instance of the first subtask in a preemptive system.

informal_sketch.intuition: The finish time of a task instance is the earliest point in time when the total processing demand (workload) for that instance has been met by the processor. This is found by iteratively increasing 't' until the workload required by 't' is less than or equal to 't' itself.
steps: Initialize 't' to an initial guess (e.g., C_i_1).
In each iteration, calculate W_i_1_k_t using Claim 5.
If W_i_1_k_t <= t, then 't' is the finish time F_i_1_k. Return 't'.
Otherwise, update 't' to W_i_1_k_t + 1 (or W_i_1_k_t if time is continuous) and repeat.
key_insights: This is a standard iterative approach for response time calculation in fixed-priority scheduling.
The convergence is guaranteed because workload is a non-decreasing function of time, and for a schedulable system, it eventually becomes less than or equal to time.

results.identifier: Claim 7: Preemptive Finish Time for tau_i_j (F_i_j_k)

formal_description.statement: F_i_j_k = min {t >= F_i_j_minus_1_k | C_i_j + M_j_k_F_i_j_minus_1_k_t + F_i_j_minus_1_k <= t}. Where M_j_k_F_i_j_minus_1_k_t = sum_{h in MP_j} ceil((t - F_i_j_minus_1_k) / T_h) * E_h.

variables.F_i_j_k: Finish time of the k-th instance of tau_i_j (from Definition 16).
variables.F_i_j_minus_1_k: Finish time of the k-th instance of the predecessor subtask tau_i_j_minus_1 (from Definition 16).
variables.C_i_j: Execution duration of subtask tau_i_j (from Definition 2).
variables.M_j_k_F_i_j_minus_1_k_t: Preemption effect from MP_j segments in the interval [F_i_j_minus_1_k, t).
variables.MP_j: MP set for subtask tau_i_j (from Definition 10).
variables.E_h: Execution duration of segment h (from Definition 8).

assumptions: Preemptive scheduling.
Analyzing subtask tau_i_j (where j > 1) in the canonical chain.
Precedence constraint: tau_i_j can only start after tau_i_j_minus_1 finishes.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an iterative equation to calculate the finish time of the k-th instance of any subtask (j > 1) in a preemptive system, considering its predecessor's completion.

informal_sketch.intuition: For any subtask after the first one, its execution cannot begin until its immediate predecessor (tau_i_j_minus_1) has completed. So, its finish time is calculated starting from F_i_j_minus_1_k, adding its own execution and any interference from higher priority MP segments that occur during its execution window.
steps: The earliest tau_i_j_k can become ready is F_i_j_minus_1_k.
Initialize 't' to F_i_j_minus_1_k + C_i_j (an initial guess for its finish time).
In each iteration, calculate the preemption effect M_j_k_F_i_j_minus_1_k_t: For each segment 'h' in MP_j, sum ceil((t - F_i_j_minus_1_k) / T_h) * E_h.
Calculate the total demand: C_i_j + M_j_k_F_i_j_minus_1_k_t + F_i_j_minus_1_k.
If this total demand is less than or equal to 't', then 't' is F_i_j_k. Return 't'.
Otherwise, update 't' to (total demand) + 1 and repeat.
key_insights: Precedence constraints are handled by making the finish time dependent on the predecessor's finish time.
Interference is only considered from the point the subtask becomes ready (F_i_j_minus_1_k).

formal_description.statement: A graph task tau_i is schedulable if r_i_ni <= D_i, where r_i_ni is the worst-case response time of the last subtask tau_i_ni in its canonical chain, and D_i is the relative deadline of the graph task.

variables.r_i_ni: Worst-case response time of the last subtask tau_i_ni (from Definition 18).
variables.D_i: Relative deadline of graph task tau_i (from Definition 1).
variables.tau_i_ni: The last subtask in the canonical chain P_i_ni_star.

assumptions: Preemptive fixed-priority scheduling.
All subtasks are preemptive.
WCRT calculations (Claims 3, 5, 6, 7, and Definitions 17, 18) are correctly applied.
formal_description.conclusion: If the last subtask of a graph task completes within the graph task's deadline, the entire graph task is schedulable.

informal_sketch.intuition: Due to precedence constraints, the entire graph task cannot complete until its very last subtask completes. Therefore, if the worst-case completion time of the last subtask is within the graph's deadline, all preceding subtasks must also have completed in time, and thus the entire graph task meets its deadline.
steps: For the graph task tau_i, identify its last subtask in the canonical chain, tau_i_ni.
Calculate the worst-case response time r_i_ni for this subtask using the preemptive WCRT analysis (Claims 3, 5, 6, 7, and Definitions 17, 18).
Compare r_i_ni with the graph task's deadline D_i.
If r_i_ni <= D_i, the graph task tau_i is schedulable.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_preemptive_schedulability(graph_task_tau_i, all_tasks_in_system):
    # 1. Transform graph to canonical chain for tau_i_ni
    canonical_chain_P_i_ni_star = transform_chain_to_canonical(graph_task_tau_i.P, graph_task_tau_i.last_subtask)
    last_subtask_tau_i_ni = canonical_chain_P_i_ni_star[-1]
    
    # 2. Create MP/SB sets for tau_i_ni
    MP_ni_set, SB_ni_set = create_interference_sets(all_tasks_in_system.chains, get_pi_i_j_star(canonical_chain_P_i_ni_star, last_subtask_tau_i_ni), last_subtask_tau_i_ni)
    
    # 3. Calculate L_i_ni (busy period length)
    L_i_ni = calculate_preemptive_L_i_j(MP_ni_set, SB_ni_set, canonical_chain_P_i_ni_star[0].C)
    
    # 4. Calculate N_i (number of activations)
    N_i = calculate_N_i(L_i_ni, graph_task_tau_i.T)
    
    # 5. Calculate F_i_j_k for all subtasks up to tau_i_ni
    finish_times_for_tau_i = {}
    for k in range(1, N_i + 1):
        # Calculate F_i_1_k
        F_i_1_k = calculate_preemptive_F_i_1_k(k, canonical_chain_P_i_ni_star[0].C, MP_ni_set, SB_ni_set, calculate_E_i_1(canonical_chain_P_i_ni_star, last_subtask_tau_i_ni))
        finish_times_for_tau_i[(canonical_chain_P_i_ni_star[0].id, k)] = F_i_1_k
        
        # Calculate F_i_j_k for j > 1
        for j_idx in range(1, len(canonical_chain_P_i_ni_star)):
            tau_i_j = canonical_chain_P_i_ni_star[j_idx]
            tau_i_j_minus_1 = canonical_chain_P_i_ni_star[j_idx-1]
            F_i_j_minus_1_k = finish_times_for_tau_i[(tau_i_j_minus_1.id, k)]
            F_i_j_k = calculate_preemptive_F_i_j_k(k, tau_i_j.C, F_i_j_minus_1_k, MP_ni_set) # MP_j_set might be different for each j
            finish_times_for_tau_i[(tau_i_j.id, k)] = F_i_j_k
            
    # 6. Calculate r_i_ni
    finish_times_ni_k = {k: finish_times_for_tau_i[(last_subtask_tau_i_ni.id, k)] for k in range(1, N_i + 1)}
    r_i_ni = calculate_WCRT(N_i, graph_task_tau_i.T, finish_times_ni_k)
    
    # 7. Check schedulability
    return r_i_ni <= graph_task_tau_i.D
key_insights: The schedulability of the entire graph task is determined by its critical path, which ends with the last subtask.
This condition is sufficient for schedulability.

    # 5. Calculate W_i_j_k and F_i_j_k for all subtasks up to tau_i_ni

        F_i_1_k = calculate_non_preemptive_F_i_1_k(W_i_1_k, canonical_chain_P_i_ni_star[0].C)
